about: THE YEAR A MERCHANT LIVES BY, 793 to 805, by faith (Design/fate_faith_and_self.md section 3: 'the calendar bites'). Written 7 Oct 2026 from Design/content/lore/saints_calendar.md, calendar.json, gods_cult.md and law_tolls.md, with the movable days reckoned afresh. All dates are Julian, as in chronicle_793.json. 'faiths' are the ids of self_793.json. 'where' is a condition in the encounter engine's language (Cond.cs: port.id, port.realm, port.people, port.faith). 'may_not' is what a keeper of that faith may not do or carry on the day; 'dear' and 'cheap' are good ids of goods_793.json whose price the day moves, with 'x' a starting guess for a price_shock. 'attested': period (a law or text of the 8th or early 9th century says it), later_law (written down after 805 but describing older custom; the source says when), later (a source long after: say 'it is said'), computed (reckoned by rule, no record), game (the game's own rule). (?) marks what was not checked. The first release is one life on twelve ports: dorestad, traiectum, walichrum, lundenwic, witla, medemelacha, doccinga, daventre, quentovic, sarre, fordwic, ripa (Design/GAME_MAKER.md stages 1 and 2). The engine already knows the main feasts (Code/Runtime/Levels/Feasts.cs); this file adds what each faith must do about them. A draft for the user to overwrite.

reckoning.easter: The Sunday after the fourteenth moon that falls on or after 21 March, taken from the nineteen-year table of Dionysius Exiguus as Bede taught it (De temporum ratione, 725). Reckoned here by the usual formula for the Julian calendar: a = year mod 4, b = year mod 7, c = year mod 19, d = (19c + 15) mod 30, e = (2a + 4b - d + 34) mod 7; month = floor((d + e + 114) / 31), day = ((d + e + 114) mod 31) + 1. Checked against two days the annals give: Easter 800 on 19 April, when Charles kept it at Saint-Riquier (ARF 800), and Easter Monday 799 on 1 April (Theophanes AM 6291). Every date below was also checked to fall on a Sunday.
reckoning.weekdays: From the Julian day number: 8 June 793 (Lindisfarne) was a Saturday; 25 December 800 a Friday; 20 July 802 (the elephant at Aachen) a Wednesday; 12 October 803 (Clofesho) a Thursday. Check: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls 16 July 809 a Monday ('ii feria') and the reckoning agrees.
reckoning.jewish_year: By the fixed calendar of the rabbis (the molad and the four postponements, as in Dershowitz and Reingold, Calendrical Calculations), turned into Julian days and checked against two modern new years. The rules were in use by the 9th century but were still argued in 921 to 922 (Saadia and Ben Meir), so a day here may be one day off what a community of 793 kept (?). A Jewish day begins at dusk the evening before the date given.
reckoning.who_uses_what: A Christian counts by feasts ('three days before Saint John'). A heathen counts winters and nights, and the moon. A Jew counts from dusk to dusk and by his own months. The frame's day rule shows the days of the player's own faith first (me.faith).

easter_by_year.note: Good Friday 802 fell on Lady Day, 25 March: the feast gives way to the fast. In 797 Easter was almost as late as it can be (23 April), so Lent ran to within two days of the Greater Litany and the hungry weeks were long. In 794 it was almost as early as it can be (23 March): Lent began on 5 February, three days after Candlemas.
easter_by_year.source: computed (see reckoning.easter); agrees with Design/content/lore/saints_calendar.md section 3 for 793, 794, 795 and 800

may_not: eat or keep leavened bread or beer aboard for the eight days: the ship's bread and the ale go ashore or are sold to a stranger first
trade on the first two and last two days
passover.source: Exodus 12:15-20; Mishnah Pesahim 1-3 (ale of barley is leaven); eight days outside the land of Israel

may_not: eat or drink from dusk to dusk
trade, load or sail by choice
day_of_atonement.note: In 793 it fell on Saturday 21 September, eight days before the count's Michaelmas reckoning; in 803 on 30 September, the day after it.

may_not: trade or load on the first two and last two days
booths.note: Meals are eaten in a booth of branches: for a moored boat, a booth on the bank.

purim.note: Gifts of food to friends and silver to the poor.

week.name: The Lord's day
week.from: Saturday dusk in Kent, by Wihtred's law; Sunday dawn elsewhere
may_not: cart goods, except food, a body for burial, or for the host
bring a suit: no court sits
week.prices: Bread, ale and fish sell on Saturday; no hands can be hired till Monday.
week.penalty: Frisia: a fine in solidi, heavier beyond the Lauwers (Lex Frisionum XVIII: 12 and 4 solidi (?)). Kent: a free man who works in the forbidden time pays his healsfang; a servant set to work by his lord costs the lord 80 sceattas (Wihtred 9-11). Wessex: a slave made to work on Sunday goes free (Ine 3).
week.source: Admonitio generalis 789 c. 81 (no servile work, with the three cartings allowed); Lex Frisionum XVIII (about 802); Wihtred 9-11 (695); Ine 3 (about 690); markets: capitulary of 809, MGH Capit. I nos. 61-62 (?) and chronicle_793.json 809-sunday-markets

week.name: Friday
may_not: eat meat (unless a feast falls on it)
week.source: old church custom; in English law only from V Aethelred 17 (1008) and I Cnut 16; Design/content/lore/saints_calendar.md section 4

week.name: Wednesday, the first fast
week.note: Kept by monks everywhere and by the Irish strictly: the Irish names of Wednesday and Friday mean 'first fast' and 'fast', and Thursday 'the day between two fasts'.
week.source: the Old Irish day names (cetain, aine, dardain); the Rule of Tallaght (9th century) (?)

week.name: The Sabbath
may_not: buy, sell, weigh or count silver
load, unload or carry a burden ashore
put to sea in the three days before it, unless the voyage is a duty
may: stay aboard a ship already under way, and let a crew of other faiths work her
week.note: A port whose market day is Saturday is closed to a Jewish merchant. About 826 bishop Agobard complained that at Lyon the market had been moved off Saturday so that the Jews need not break their Sabbath: do not show that favour in a port of 793.
week.source: Exodus 20:8-11; 35:3; Mishnah Shabbat 7:2; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 19a (no setting out by ship less than three days before the Sabbath) (?); Agobard, De insolentia Iudaeorum (about 826-827)

week.name: Washing day
week.note: The Northmen's name for Saturday is 'washing day' (Old Norse laugardagr). A wash, a comb and a clean shirt before a hall is worth a pip of Name for that day (the game's rule). The English complaint that the Danes combed daily, bathed every Saturday and changed their clothes often, and so won English women, is in the chronicle that goes under John of Wallingford's name, written in the 13th century about the years before 1002: LATER.
week.source: Old Norse laugardagr (written 12th century and after); the chronicle attributed to John of Wallingford (13th century)

week.name: The moon and the tide
week.note: Springs at full and new moon; high water at a different hour in each port. Every faith counts by the moon: Easter and Passover hang on the same spring moon, and the heathen north counts its feasts by it.

fixed.name: The octave of the Lord
may_not: keep the heathen new year with gifts and masks
fixed.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36 (the list of feasts to be kept, written eight years after this life ends: older custom)

fixed.name: Epiphany, the Twelfth Day
fixed.note: The twelve days end. The priest gives out the date of Easter (?): from now every port knows when fish will be wanted.

fixed.name: Candlemas, the Purification
fixed.note: Candles are blessed and carried. Buy fish for Lent now and look the ship over.

fixed.name: Saint Gregory
fixed.note: The pope who sent the faith to the English. Falls in Lent in most years: a feast without meat.

fixed.name: The Annunciation, Lady Day
fixed.note: In Lent in most years (after Easter only in 794, in Holy Week in 799 and 804), and on Good Friday itself in 802.
fixed.source: V Aethelred 14 (1008) for the fast before it; kept at Rome from the 7th century

fixed.name: The Greater Litany
may_not: work or trade until the procession is home
fixed.note: A procession round the fields with relics. On this day in 799 pope Leo was set upon in Rome.

fixed.name: Philip and James
fixed.note: A feast with meat, because it lies in Easter time. If the game begins on 1 May 793 (fate, section 6b) it begins on this feast, a Wednesday.

fixed.name: Saint Augustine of Canterbury
fixed.note: Canterbury's own day: a crowd at the abbey of the kings' graves, a mile up the track from the hythe.

fixed.name: Saint Boniface and his companions
fixed.where: port.id = doccinga or port.id = traiectum or port.id = medemelacha
fixed.note: Killed at Doccinga on 5 June 754: pilgrims come by boat to the church and the spring. In 793 it fell three days before Lindisfarne.
fixed.source: Willibald, Vita Bonifatii c. 8; Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I

fixed.name: The eve of Saint John
fixed.note: Fires on the eve are well known later and likely now (?).
fixed.source: V Aethelred 14 (the fast before a feast); Design/content/spine.json calendar

fixed.name: Saint John the Baptist, at midsummer
fixed.note: The great feast of the sailing months: every town full and off its guard.

fixed.name: Saints Peter and Paul
fixed.note: The patronal day of Saint Paul's at Lundenwic: a crowd there on the days around it.

fixed.name: Saint Martin in summer
fixed.note: The summer feast of Saint Martin's churches: a gathering at Traiectum in the months when ships can reach it.

fixed.name: Saint Mildrith of Thanet
fixed.note: The day of the minster on Thanet, whose abbess has the toll on her own ships at Sarre and Fordwic by the kings' charters.
fixed.source: the Kentish toll charters for the abbesses of Thanet (S 29 of 763 or 764 (?); S 86 and others (?)); the Mildrith legend is written down later

fixed.name: Lammas, the loaf-mass, on Saint Peter's Chains
fixed.note: A loaf of the new corn is blessed. Harvest has begun: grain is about to fall and no hands can be hired. The English name is written from the 9th century, so likely in 793 (?).

fixed.name: The Assumption of Saint Mary
fixed.note: Harvest in full swing; honey is taken.

fixed.name: Michaelmas: the reckoning
fixed.note: The day the house's debt falls due (the game's rule: that Dorestat reckoned debts on it in 793 is not recorded). The harvest is sold; the autumn gales begin. A count who is owed sits to be paid on a feast, and may not hear a suit that day.
fixed.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36 (the feast); Design/DECISIONS.md no. 10 (the debt); saints_calendar.md section 10

fixed.name: Saint Remigius
fixed.note: A Frankish feast of the first rank and a rent day on many estates (?). The vintage begins on the Rhine.

fixed.name: All Saints
fixed.where: port.people = english or (port.realm = franks and year >= 800)
fixed.note: English and Irish in 793. Alcuin urges it on his Frankish friends about 800; it is ordered for the whole realm only in 835. Do not put it in a Frankish mouth before 800.
fixed.source: Alcuin's letter to Arn of Salzburg, 800 (MGH Epistolae IV no. 193 (?)); Design/content/spine.json calendar

fixed.name: Saint Willibrord
fixed.note: He died in 739. At Walichrum he broke an idol and its keeper struck him on the head with a sword: the place where it stood is still shown.

fixed.name: Martinmas
fixed.note: The sea shuts: the end of the game's sailing year, by the old rule every clerk could read. The slaughter month: salt is dearest, hides and beasts cheap, the new wine comes down the Rhine. Martinmas week, 7 to 11 November, is Traiectum's high time; servants are hired and let go.
fixed.source: Vegetius, Epitoma rei militaris IV.39 (the seas shut from 11 November to 10 March); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15 (Blotmonath); Council of Mainz 813 c. 36

fixed.name: Saint Lebuin
fixed.note: He died about 775; the Saxons burned his church and Liudger built it again. One day after Martinmas: the two feasts make one gathering on the IJssel.

fixed.name: Saint Andrew
fixed.note: The fast before Christmas begins about now in most churches.

fixed.name: Saint Josse
fixed.note: The cell of Saint Josse by Quentovic, a hospice for travellers from over the sea, said to have been given to Alcuin about 792 (?).
fixed.source: Lupus of Ferrieres, letters (about 840), on the cell given to Alcuin for the reception of strangers (?); dossier quentovic.md

fixed.name: Christmas
may_not: work or trade for four days
fixed.note: Four days kept whole, twelve of feasting. The Frankish annals turn the year here: the 'year 801' of the royal annals begins on Christmas Day 800, the day Charles was crowned emperor.

movable.name: Septuagesima
movable.note: The Alleluia is laid aside. In later English law no oaths or ordeals from now until two weeks after Easter: a merchant who needs an oath to clear himself may wait two months for it.

movable.name: Ash Wednesday: Lent begins
movable.note: Forty fast days: one meal, late, and no flesh. Fish is wanted before and through it; meat, cheese, butter and eggs do not sell. In Saxony, by the first law for the conquered, a man who ate meat in Lent 'in contempt of the Christian faith' was to die unless a priest judged it need; Daventre lies on that border.
movable.source: Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 4 (about 782-785); Wihtred 14-15 (695); Theodulf of Orleans, Capitula I (about 800) (?)

movable.name: Palm Sunday
movable.note: Processions with branches: willow and yew in the north.

movable.name: Good Friday
may_not: eat before evening, and then only bread and water
movable.note: The black fast. No mass, no bell, no market.

movable.name: Holy Saturday
movable.note: The vigil and the great day for baptisms: the new Christians wear white, and fine linen sells before it (?). A prime-signed player who is baptised this night leaves that faith for good.
movable.source: Notker, Gesta Karoli II.19 (about 885: Northmen baptised more than once for the white clothes); Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 19 (infants to be baptised within the year)

movable.name: Easter
may_not: work or trade through Easter week
movable.note: The year's first feast and the end of the fast: wine for every altar, new clothes, meat again, and the sea opens. The crew is hired and sworn about now. After it come the hungry weeks: grain is dearest in April and May.
movable.source: Council of Mainz 813 c. 36 (Easter week kept whole); seasons_793.json

movable.name: The Rogation days
may_not: work until the procession is home
movable.note: Monday to Wednesday before the Ascension: the fields are walked with the cross and the relics.
movable.source: Council of Orleans 511 c. 27; Council of Clofesho 747 c. 16

movable.name: The Ascension
movable.note: The first crossings to England are made about now.

movable.name: Pentecost, or Whitsun
may_not: work or trade through the week
movable.note: Kept like Easter; the second day for baptisms. Wool is shorn about now and the long voyages start.

fasts.name: Lent
fasts.rule: No flesh of beast or bird; by the strict rule no milk, butter, cheese or eggs. One meal, after vespers or, by now, in mid-afternoon. Ale and wine are drink, not food. Whale and porpoise count as fish.
fasts.excused: children, the old, the sick, women with child, and those at heavy work or on a hard journey, by a priest's leave (?): a crew at sea in Lent is a fair case, and the fish is to hand anyway

fasts.name: The fasts of the four seasons
fasts.rule: A Wednesday, Friday and Saturday in each season. The weeks were not the same everywhere: the council of Mainz of 813 fixed them for the Frankish realm as the first week of March, the second of June, the third of September and the full week before Christmas eve.

fasts.name: The fast before Christmas, Saint Martin's Lent
fasts.rule: Lighter than Lent and not the same in any two dioceses: in Gaul by old rule three days a week; monks keep it whole.
fasts.source: Council of Macon 581 c. 9 (?); saints_calendar.md section 4

fasts.name: The three Lents of the Irish
fasts.rule: A winter Lent before Christmas, the spring Lent, and a summer Lent after Pentecost, kept by the stricter Irish houses.

fasts.name: Horse flesh
fasts.rule: Never eaten. It is on the table at every heathen feast: what is on the board tells a guest where he is.
fasts.source: pope Gregory III to Boniface, about 732 (Boniface, letter 28); the legates' report of 786 c. 19

heathen.name: The feast at the start of winter
heathen.when: mid October; the game's day for Ripa: 14 October (?)
heathen.what: A beast killed, the meat shared, ale brewed for it. Raiders are home; hire and fostering run from now to summer.
may_not: turn a guest from the board
heathen.what_is_sure: That the heathen north feasted at the start of winter: a Christian poet riding east in autumn about 1019 was turned from farm after farm because the households were 'keeping the elves' sacrifice'. The name 'winter nights' and the three feasts a year are Snorri's, about 1230.
heathen.source: Sigvat, Austrfararvisur (about 1019); Snorri, Ynglinga saga c. 8 (about 1230); saints_calendar.md section 8

heathen.name: Yule
heathen.when: midwinter; the night is not known for 793 (later accounts put it after Christmas, in January)
heathen.what: Ale drunk, pork eaten, oaths sworn. Yule is 'drunk': that much is sure.
heathen.what_is_sure: A king means 'to drink Yule at sea' in a poem of about 900. Bede says the heathen English began their year on 25 December with 'mothers' night'. Thietmar, writing 1012 to 1018 at second hand, puts a great feast at Lejre every ninth year in January, after the Epiphany.
heathen.source: Haraldskvaedi (about 900); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15 (725); Thietmar of Merseburg I.17

heathen.name: The February doings
heathen.what: Among the lately baptised Frisians and Saxons the priests' list of forbidden things names 'the filthy doings in February', feasts at graves and offerings at springs and trees. Bede's February is 'the month of cakes' offered to the gods. No day is given.
may_not: be seen at it in a Frankish port: it is the count's business in Saxony and the priest's in Frisia
heathen.source: Indiculus superstitionum et paganiarum, heads 1-3, 11 (about 743, in a manuscript of about 800); Bede, De temporum ratione c. 15

heathen.name: The feast at the start of summer
heathen.when: mid April; the game's day for Ripa: 14 April (?)
heathen.what: The ships are launched and an offering made for the season. Lots are cast before a voyage to learn whether the gods will help.
heathen.what_is_sure: Lots before a voyage are in Rimbert (of the 850s). Adam of Bremen, about 1075, puts the great nine-yearly feast of the Svear at Uppsala about the spring equinox. A spring 'sacrifice for victory' is Snorri's.
heathen.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 18-19, 27, 30; Adam of Bremen IV.27 and its note; Snorri, Ynglinga saga c. 8

heathen.name: The darkened moon
heathen.when: at an eclipse of the moon seen from the port: 28 March 796 before dawn; 21 September 796 in the evening; 5 February 798 in the evening; 15 January 800 in the evening; 21 May 802 before dawn; the night of 2 to 3 November 803; 12 September 805 at moonrise
heathen.what: People shout to help the moon: 'Win, moon!' A Christian crew is forbidden to join in; a heathen one will not stop.
heathen.source: Indiculus superstitionum, head 21 ('de lunae defectione, quod dicunt Vince luna'); the eclipses are in rare_793.json

heathen.name: The town's feast for its god
heathen.what: The town eats and drinks to honour its god, and a man who has killed a beast hangs it on a pole before his door so that all know he has made his offering.
heathen.what_is_sure: Seen at Hedeby about 965 by a traveller from Tortosa. Shown at Ripa in the 790s it is a guess (?).
heathen.source: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub al-Turtushi (about 965), in al-Qazwini

fairs_and_things.name: The summer market at Ripa
fairs_and_things.what: The plots on the bank are let and worked by season: beads, combs, bronze casting, amber, cattle, Frisian cloth and Rhenish pots. Outside these weeks the landing is half empty.
fairs_and_things.source: the digs at Ribe (plots laid out about 705 and used by season); the days are the game's (fairs_793.json: day 145, eighty days)

fairs_and_things.name: The fair of Saint-Denis
fairs_and_things.what: English ('Saxon') and Frisian merchants sell cloth and buy wine, honey and madder; the abbey takes the tolls. Outside the twelve ports: a rumour and a price in the first release.
fairs_and_things.source: the judgement of 710 and the charters of Pippin (753) and Charles (775) on the fair's tolls; dossier parisius.md

fairs_and_things.name: The gathering at Boniface's church
fairs_and_things.what: Pilgrims by boat, pedlars and the lord's men in one yard.

fairs_and_things.name: Martinmas week at Traiectum
fairs_and_things.what: Willibrord's day to Lebuin's: the see's high time, and the last market before the sea shuts.

fairs_and_things.name: The count's court, the mallus
fairs_and_things.when: the general sittings: one about summer and one about autumn in the capitulary of 769, three a year later (?). The game's days: the Monday after Low Sunday, the Monday after Saint John, the Monday after Saint Remigius.
fairs_and_things.what: Debts and thefts are heard, oaths sworn with oath-helpers, fines set. Not on a Sunday or a feast.
fairs_and_things.source: Capitulare primum 769 c. 12 (?); Lex Frisionum (about 802); the days are the game's

fairs_and_things.name: The king's assembly and the host
fairs_and_things.when: between May and August, where the king is, before the summer's campaign

by_year.793: none: the king is at Regensburg all year, digging the canal between Altmuhl and Rednitz
by_year.794: Frankfurt, about 1 June, with the great synod
by_year.795: Kostheim by Mainz, then into Saxony
by_year.797: Saxony to Hadeln on the sea; a second meeting at Aachen, 28 October
by_year.799: Lippeham on the Rhine, then Paderborn
by_year.801: none north of the Alps: the emperor is in Italy until summer
by_year.802: Aachen, in spring (the oath) and again in October (the laws)
by_year.804: Lippspringe (?), then to the Elbe at Hollenstedt

fairs_and_things.what: The great men gather and the army marches from it, to Saxony in most years to 804: grain, horses and carts are bought up along its road and counts are away from home.

fairs_and_things.name: Where the king keeps Christmas and Easter

by_year.793: Easter at Regensburg; Christmas at Wurzburg
by_year.794: Easter at Frankfurt; Christmas at Aachen
by_year.797: Easter at Aachen; Christmas at Herstelle on the Weser
by_year.798: Easter at Herstelle; Christmas at Aachen
by_year.800: Easter at Saint-Riquier, a day's ride from Quentovic; Christmas at Rome
by_year.801: Easter at Rome; Christmas at Aachen
by_year.804: Easter at Aachen (?); Christmas at Quierzy with pope Leo
by_year.805: Easter at Aachen (?); Christmas at Thionville

fairs_and_things.what: A court eats a district bare and pays for wine, wax, spices and furs. Easter 800 is the one time in this life the king himself comes within reach of the twelve ports.

fairs_and_things.name: The bishops' meetings

dated.what: prices of grain and bread fixed; the new penny to be taken everywhere
the peoples' laws read and written: the Law of the Frisians is set down about now
the archbishopric of Lichfield ended; Canterbury has the whole south again

fairs_and_things.source: MGH Capit. I no. 28; Ann. Lauresh. 802; Acts of Clofesho 803 (Birch 310, 312)

fairs_and_things.name: What is not there
fairs_and_things.what: No thing of all the Frisians is attested in the period (the Upstalsboom is 13th century). No thing at Ripa is described by anyone of the time. The Saxons' yearly meeting at Marklo is forbidden since about 785. No fair with a charter and a date is known at any of the twelve ports: their trade is the standing market under a reeve's eye, and the saints' feasts.
fairs_and_things.source: saints_calendar.md sections 6 and 7; Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae c. 34
